news.title: OpenAI and Poland’s NASK partner to advance AI safety and security
news.summary_raw: OpenAI and Poland’s NASK are partnering on AI safety, security, and technical research to strengthen safeguards and support a more resilient digital ecosystem.
news.source_text:
OpenAI and Poland’s NASK partner to advance AI safety and security
OpenAI and Poland’s NASK National Research Institute have signed an agreement to explore collaboration on AI safety, security and technical research. The partnership will bring together expertise from both organizations to better understand emerging risks, strengthen safeguards, and explore how advanced AI can contribute to a more secure and resilient digital ecosystem.
As AI systems become more capable, international collaboration between developers and public research institutions will be essential to understanding their risks and building stronger safeguards. OpenAI’s existing work with the US Center for Advancing Standards and Innovation for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), UK AI Security Institute (AISI) and other public research institutions around the world has already helped strengthen safeguards, identify and fix security vulnerabilities in AI agents, and advance frontier AI safety.
Through the agreement, NASK’s AI Safety Research Center – serving as the Polish Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (AISI) – and OpenAI will collaborate on AI safety research, exploring ways to evaluate increasingly capable AI systems, identify potential vulnerabilities and strengthen safeguards.
OpenAI has called for the US to work with countries around the world on international technical standards for frontier AI, drawing on the expertise of AI safety institutes and standards bodies. Common approaches to evaluating capabilities, assessing risks, testing safeguards and reporting incidents can help countries compare evidence and respond to risks that cross borders. The collaboration with NASK reflects the value of bringing national expertise into this wider effort.
In NASK’s case, this expertise rests on extensive research in AI safety, applied directly to protecting public services and Poland’s digital information ecosystem. Without national partners like NASK, global AI safety standards may remain detached from the realities in which AI is actually used.
The agreement also builds on OpenAI’s existing work with cyber defenders in Poland. In July, CERT Polska, which operates within NASK, gained access(opens in a new window) to OpenAI’s cyber capable models through Daybreak. The team used OpenAI models to help discover six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, including flaws that could be combined to take control of affected devices without authentication. The vendor released fixes, which CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it observed.
news.summary: OpenAI has partnered with Poland’s NASK National Research Institute to jointly advance AI safety and security research, aiming to identify and mitigate emerging AI risks. The collaboration focuses on strengthening safeguards, evaluating capabilities, and sharing incident reporting frameworks for a more resilient digital ecosystem.

news.title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
news.source_text:
Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?
The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.
Look up a model
The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.
To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.
At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to
text-generationandimage-text-to-textmodels. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.
Run it yourself
Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").
On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:
python3 run.py
No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.
A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:
hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache
What "runs" means
Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

news.title: Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)
news.summary_raw: Learn how OpenAI scaled Habitat with reliable multi-tenancy, global caching, and Azure Cosmos DB to deliver 12× faster reads for ChatGPT.
news.source_text:
Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)
How we optimized Azure Cosmos DB in our application storage platform, Habitat, to manage unprecedented growth.
All OpenAI products require fast, reliable access to data, provided by our storage platform, Habitat. It has to respond in milliseconds to over 1 billion users across 40 geographic regions. Our infrastructure faced an extraordinary challenge: supporting explosive growth and new use cases while continuing to improve reliability, performance, and product developer velocity. Solving that challenge required rethinking how our online storage platform was designed and operated. We constantly evaluated tradeoffs, following the pattern of: first become reliable enough for mission-critical product traffic, then fast enough for global users, and, finally, to deftly operate at massive scale.
This two-part series explains how we developed Habitat from a simple client library and database into a globally distributed storage platform serving over 500 petabytes of data. Part I focused on Habitat’s evolution from a Python client to a service. It also covered the techniques that allowed us to push a Python-based service far beyond what many would consider practical.
In this post, Part II, we walk through how we scaled the underlying storage component: Azure Cosmos DB. Through a close working partnership with the Azure team, we arrived at a viable multi-tenancy approach of co-managed containers, with excellent read performance at massive, global scale.
As companies scale, infra teams often evolve from running single-tenant systems to multi-tenant ones. Single-tenancy, where every product surface team maintains their own system, reduces blast radius and provides easy ownership boundaries and workload isolation. As teams and product surfaces grow, this becomes expensive to run. Single-tenancy makes every product team responsible for capacity planning and often results in significant over-provisioning.
Conversely, multi-tenancy assigns control to a centralized database team, with better knowledge and experience for provisioning resources. But multi-tenancy creates its own problems, such as noisy-neighbor issues, where one tenant consumes an unusually large share of the resources to the detriment of the other tenants.
In Habitat, we had to weigh all these tradeoffs to design a reliable, efficient, storage system at scale. Today, Habitat is a multi-tenant database layer for many OpenAI products, but we went through a circular journey from using one multi-tenant Azure Cosmos DB container to provisioning single-tenant backing containers to reverting to a multi-tenant container by default. We’re still very early in our multi-tenancy story on Habitat: we support a large set of use cases, but we’ve been able to defer investment in this area by leveraging Azure Cosmos DB’s built-in primitives wherever possible.

Tuberculosis remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases, claiming an estimated 1.23 million lives each year. Despite decades of global investment, too many cases go undetected in the communities that carry the highest burden. Over the past five years, we’ve worked to change that trajectory, moving from early research benchmarks toward open foundation models that could be tuned and deployed at the point of care.
Getting access to timely healthcare often comes down to an accident of geography: where you live, what resources your local clinic possesses, and whether a specialist is within reach.
Nowhere is this disparity more acute than in the fight against tuberculosis (TB). Despite being preventable and curable, TB claims more than 1.23 million lives annually. news.title: Empowering frontline maternal care with AI-assisted ultrasound
news.summary_raw: Health & Bioscience
news.source_text:
October 21, 2026
Angelica Willis, Research Engineer, Google Research, and Nichole Young-Lin, Clinical Lead, Google for Health
A prospective multi-center study demonstrates how AI-based blind sweep ultrasound assessment can enable non-sonographer operators with low-cost probes to deliver expert-level gestational age assessments, marking a significant step toward expanding life-saving maternal care globally.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that more than 250,000 preventable deaths occur worldwide each year due to pregnancy-related complications. While prenatal ultrasound can improve outcomes and reduce fetal and maternal mortality, two-thirds of people globally lack access to diagnostic medical imaging like ultrasound. Current methods that support maternal health rely heavily on specialized clinical training, leaving millions in low-resource settings without access to a single ultrasound during their entire pregnancy.
We saw an opportunity to conduct research towards addressing this real-world need, by developing machine learning systems that interpret "blind sweep" ultrasounds. This way of scanning allows frontline healthcare workers without specialized sonography training to perform scans by simply gliding low-cost, portable ultrasound probes across the abdomen in a standardized pattern.
Because many regions face critical shortages of experts, and traditional sonographer training is both expensive and requires a multi-year commitment, enabling these health workers to perform assessments with minimal training has the potential to significantly expand prenatal screening coverage.
Combining the minimal training requirement with AI interpretations could ultimately mean a successfully developed tool that has the potential to increase availability of ultrasound-based pregnancy assessment, and thereby improve access to higher quality maternal health.
In “Generalization of AI-Based Gestational Age Assessment Using Blind Sweep Ultrasonography”, published in JAMA Network Open, we evaluated how effectively an AI model for gestational age assessment (how far along the pregnancy is) generalizes across diverse clinical settings and hardware. While our previous research validated the model's performance on unseen patients from the same retrospective cohort it learned from, this new prospective study shows how the AI system performs reliably running live on mobile devices in real clinics, with only novice operators and unfamiliar ultrasound equipment, and minimal fine-tuning.
“The gestational age is basically how far along a woman is in pregnancy. All of our screening, a lot of our treatments, a lot of our indications for delivery are all based on this master timeline that you get from the gestational age.”

news.title: Beyond tree cover: mapping the world’s forest types
news.summary_raw: A global map categorizing every 10-meter patch of land on Earth into distinct forest types.
news.source_text:
Beyond tree cover: mapping the world’s forest types
A new 10-meter resolution map shows which of the world's forests are natural, planted, or farmed, and how they are changing over time
Protecting the planet's forests starts with a simple question: what type of forest are we looking at? From space, an old-growth rainforest, a eucalyptus plantation, and an oil palm estate can look like the same patch of green. But they hold very different amounts of carbon and biodiversity. Telling them apart, and knowing how each patch has changed over time, shows us where conservation is working and where natural forests are being converted into plantations and farms.
Today, Google DeepMind and Google Research, together with the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), are releasing Forest Typology (ForTy) 2020, a global map that categorizes every 10-by-10-meter patch of land on Earth into six distinct forest and land-use types, a key baseline for the EU's deforestation regulation. Alongside it, we're sharing an early time series that tracks how these forests changed each year from 2017 to 2025, including where natural forests were replaced by plantations or farms. For the first time, users can see at 10-meter detail worldwide, year by year, not just where forest was lost, but what replaced it: a timber plantation, a tree-crop farm or other land.
Why "tree cover" isn't enough
All forests store carbon and, together, forests are home to most of the world's land-based plant and animal species. But a forest’s ecological value also depends on its history: a primary forest that has never been cleared holds far more carbon and biodiversity than a single-species timber plantation that is harvested every decade or two.
Most global maps only indicate whether trees are present. That's a challenge for those trying to protect natural forests. The European Union's regulation on deforestation-free products (EUDR), for example, requires that products like coffee, cocoa or palm oil do not originate from land that was forest in 2020 and has since been converted to agriculture. Similarly, wood products, such as furniture, must also be free of forest degradation: they can't come from primary forests that have since been converted into plantation or planted forests, or from naturally regenerating forests that have since been converted into plantation forests. As a result, companies and regulators need to know not just where trees are, but what kind of forest they form (primary or regrowing, planted or plantation, forest or farm) and what replaces that forest after a harvest.
Last year, we jointly released Natural Forests of the World 2020, a 10-meter resolution global map that separated natural forests from all other tree cover. It offered a starting point to help companies and regulators implement the EU Deforestation Regulation, and to support commodity producers in meeting their commitments not to convert natural forest

This data supports compliance with the EU deforestation‑free product regulation by distinguishing natural forests from plantations and farms.

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.
We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts.
We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.
Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.
Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+
So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.
Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.
We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.
What happened after training
We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
New antibiotics are urgently needed to help with rising levels of antimicrobial resistance, but searching for new therapeutics is often a slow, labor-intensive process. With Google Antigravity, our agentic development platform, this process can now be made easier.
Google Antigravity provides an agentic science workbench that empowers biologists to discover, structurally evaluate, and prioritize promising targets quickly, compressing what used to be a fragmented search over multiple databases into a single session. It also helps researchers scan through millions of previously uncharacterized proteins in the UniProt database using ProtNLM, a model that predicts biological function from amino acid sequences.
This technical walkthrough shows how biologists used Google Antigravity to uncover a novel antimicrobial peptide candidate which has predicted activity against the pathogens involved in respiratory tract infections. The lead identified here is now undergoing wet-lab validation.
Finding new antimicrobial peptides
Rising antimicrobial resistance is one of the most pressing global health crises of our time and could result in an estimated 10 million annual deaths globally by 2050. To prevent this, we urgently need to discover novel therapeutics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly bacteriocins, offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics because they have naturally evolved to target fundamental vulnerabilities in competing bacteria, from cell envelopes to essential intracellular machinery, making it difficult for pathogens to develop resistance.
The exponential growth of genomic and metagenomic sequencing has populated global databases with billions of natural amino acid sequences. This pool of natural data has already produced globally used bacteriocins like Nisin, alongside recent genome-mined breakthroughs such as Darobactin, Dynobactin, and Lariocidin.
Many, however, remain locked within the unannotated "dark matter" of protein databases, with their function uncharacterized because they aren’t similar to known proteins. For example, the world's leading public resource of protein sequence and functional information, UniProt, holds millions of sequences with unknown functionality, transferred directly from genome sequencing projects.
To bridge this gap, Google developed ProtNLM (Protein Natural Language Model), a deep learning model trained to directly read the underlying evolutionary “grammar” of amino acid sequences. This allows the model to predict biological function directly from raw protein sequences, enriching millions of previously unnamed UniProt entries with high-confidence functional labels.

news.source_text:
LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
📄 Paper
Encountering a new paper can change a research idea's trajectory. The researcher may discover that someone has already addressed their proposed contribution, or find an unresolved problem in the paper that inspires a new direction of inquiry.
We call this process a literature-initiated pivot: a change in research direction prompted by reading prior work. It connects two activities that researchers often have to manage separately: developing an idea and deciding which literature to measure it against.
With collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania, we developed LitPivot, a system that helps researchers navigate these pivots. Using papers retrieved through Asta Paper Finder, LitPivot organizes literature around the part of a proposal being edited, offers critiques supported by excerpts from selected studies, and suggests revisions that researchers can accept, edit, or reject. LitPivot is intended to be used for early-stage research ideation, but the idea could possibly extend to longer writing tasks (i.e., writing the introduction section of a paper).
In a study with 17 researchers, domain experts rated research ideas developed with LitPivot as better grounded in the literature than those developed with a text editor and an AI chat tool. Participants also perceived their revised research ideas as more novel and useful, and reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature.
LitPivot will be presented at UIST 2026 in Detroit. Read the paper here.
Why pivoting is hard
Research ideas evolve through engaging with the literature. In our analysis of meeting notes from four completed computer science research projects, we identified 21 literature-initiated pivots across all four projects. These fell into two types: differentiating an idea from existing work to establish an idea’s novelty, and aligning an idea with existing work to build on it. This project itself went through two pivots before we settled on its contributions.
These changes can be difficult to navigate. In a formative study, five researchers developed proposals using a text editor and standard search tools. They struggled to develop their ideas while critically evaluating them against the literature. When a paper challenged an idea’s novelty, they wanted concrete suggestions for how to revise it, supported by prior work. These findings shaped LitPivot’s assessments, which pair literature-supported critiques with specific suggestions for revising the selected part of an idea.

In LitPivot, a researcher starts by writing a short proposal in an editor and enabling what we call facet highlighting, which segments an articulated idea into different facets (i.e., a problem, contribution, and evaluation). Unlock FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards to their professional equivalents
This Linux kernel module combines the CMP unlocker's V67/PLM technique with the pre-driver timing of the UEFI approach. It runs the unlock, writes the speed selectors (SS0 0x88888888, which selects the full BF16 rate, and the 4-bit SS1 0x8 IMLA4) and performs FLR before the unmodified NVIDIA driver binds the card. It is neither a UEFI application nor a patched NVIDIA driver.
The benefit of this early kmod driver is that it does not require manual patching each time nvidia releases a new driver version.
The effect of this unlock is that it doubles the instruction issuing speed of FP/BF16 FMA into FP32 operations on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards.
3090 Ti dense 8192³ GEMM at 450 W, five-sample medians with FP32 accumulation:
Results reported by users. The module accepts every GeForce ID listed in
kernel/gpu_unlock/main.c, but the cards below are the ones someone has
reported on. Please add yours with a
compatibility report,
whether it worked or not.
The gains are dense GEMM throughput from each report's own benchmark, so they are not directly comparable. The power limit matters a lot: the lowest figure (+25%) is from cards capped at 225 W.
Matrix-heavy work speeds up: LLM prefill (+14–36% in #9, #15, #25 and #33), diffusion and FlashAttention. LLM decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth, and INT8 work stay about the same. The reports that compared outputs found them bit-identical before and after.
Reports also cover up to four cards in one machine, the card driving the display, and cards passed through to a VM with vfio-pci (#17).
First run:
git clone https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock
cd gpu-unlock
make installThen append gpu_unlock.targets=all to your kernel command line, keeping
existing options:
- GRUB (Debian/Ubuntu/Mint): add it inside GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULTin/etc/default/grub, then runsudo update-grub.
- GRUB (Arch/CachyOS): same edit, then run
sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg.
- Fedora/RHEL: run
sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="gpu_unlock.targets=all".
- systemd-boot: append it to the optionsline in your boot entry (bootctl statusshows its location).
- UKI / generated entries: add it to /etc/kernel/cmdlineand regenerate your boot images/entries (e.g.sudo mkinitcpio -Pfor mkinitcpio UKIs).
Every build downloads the pinned NVIDIA/CachyOS inputs over HTTPS, checks
their SHA-256, and generates firmware only in the build directory and the
binary package. All three formats install through the same make install-*
targets. Packages are built from the committed HEAD.
Build, install build dependencies, and install the packages in one step (asks for your sudo password):
make install        # detect the distribution and select an installer
make install-arch   # makepkg -sif
make install-deb    # apt-get build-dep, dpkg-buildpackage, apt-get install
make install-rpm    # dnf builddep, rpmbuild, dnf installmake install uses /etc

news.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
news.summary_raw: For 3 days this month, 333 exit nodes were hacked in hopes of stealing sensitive data.
news.source_text:
Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday.
The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers, the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury, a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago.
Mysteries remain
Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.
Ultimately, 333 exit relays were involved in the SSH and email interception campaign, although investigators haven’t established how the attackers gained control of all the underlying servers. The attackers then reconfigured the servers. One set of changes redirected SSH traffic traversing Tor to one of 12 attacker-controlled interceptor servers. Tor users who ignored warnings that the SSH host key had changed would then enter their SSH passwords.
A second set of changes caused the exit nodes to block ports 25, 465, 587, 993, and 995—used to accept various forms of encrypted email—while continuing to allow ports for receiving unencrypted email. If email services downgraded the connections, the attackers used their access to the exit nodes to obtain unencrypted messages. It’s unclear whether any such downgrade attempts succeeded. The hijacking occurred from October 2 to October 5.
Tor volunteers partially outlined the initial compromise of the management server and Switzerland2 and the attempt to intercept unencrypted email. Tuesday’s report revealed many new details, including how many exit nodes were compromised and how the attackers used them to redirect SSH traffic.

That’s exactly what happened to me on Friday morning.” Kaba then received the following warning:

news.title: Democratic governance of frontier AI, part II: Empowering cyber defenders
news.summary_raw: OpenAI outlines a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders with frontier AI, stronger safeguards, modernized cybersecurity, and more resilient public institutions.
news.source_text:
Democratic governance of frontier AI, part II: Empowering cyber defenders
AI is changing the speed, scale, and economics of cybersecurity. It can help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, detect intrusions, and respond to attacks—but those same capabilities can enable malicious actors and create new risks when AI systems act beyond their intended boundaries. We are in a defender’s window: a limited opportunity to put advanced AI into defenders’ hands and strengthen protections before advanced cyber offensive capabilities become widely available.
Today, we’re publishing a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders, building on our earlier cybersecurity action plan and frontier safety blueprint(opens in a new window). Our experience with misalignment and security incidents involving our own models underscores the need for stronger safeguards and accountability across the industry. Drawing on those lessons, the blueprint puts forward concrete proposals for governments and industry in three areas:
- Strengthening safety and security for advanced AI: Establish clearer responsibilities for securing frontier models and agents, detecting dangerous behavior, and maintaining reliable shutdown controls for operations under each organization’s control. 
- Modernizing cybersecurity for the intelligence age: Equip defenders with advanced tools, training, and technical support; address longstanding cybersecurity weaknesses; and invest in securing essential services and replacing outdated systems. 
- Building resilient and adaptive public institutions: Strengthen government evaluations and independent technical assessments, establish consistent incident reporting requirements, and improve coordinated response and recovery. 
AI labs have a responsibility to address the risks their systems create and help strengthen society’s defenses. Governments must also have the expertise, resources, and authority to protect the public as capabilities advance. We encourage policymakers to act now—establishing safeguards, learning from experience, and strengthening requirements as the technology evolves.

news.title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse
news.summary_raw: Survey of 2,018 IT heads at big firms points to a lack of leverage.
news.source_text:
Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms’ IT heads think those changes are detrimental.
Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “The Software Tax.” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue.
Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. A third-party research consultancy, Censuswide, conducted the survey.
Among the report’s most concerning findings, enterprises often make software purchases that IT heads believe could hurt the organization. Ninety-five percent of respondents said “their organization has paid for a vendor-driven upgrade, migration, or licensing change in the past three years that it believed at the time would reduce performance, reliability, or business value,” the report says. Fifty-three percent of respondents “have done so more than once,” the report notes.
“Some 76 percent say their organization has very little real leverage in negotiations, and 80 percent say moving away from major vendors would cause significant disruption,” the report says, referring to the share of respondents who selected “strongly agree” or “somewhat agree” to those statements.

news.title: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
news.source_text:
Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.
Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔
TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.
TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.
The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.
The old way
Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.
To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.
Enter TorchTPU 🚀
TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:
pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.
Your favourite libraries, now on TPU
Transformers
Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="tpu", # will load model directly on the TPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
inputs = tokenizer("The future of AI is", return_tensors="pt").to("tpu")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.
Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨
TPU is now a first-class d
news.summary: Hugging Face has released TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend that enables running Transformers, Diffusers, and other Hugging Face models directly on Google Cloud TPUs without the need for torch_xla or JAX. This simplifies AI model deployment and training on TPUs by allowing developers to use standard PyTorch code with device_map="tpu".

news.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
news.summary_raw: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
news.source_text:
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.
More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching.
Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.
The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.
OpenAI has taken several stumbles
Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “super app.” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”
The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after, bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.
That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.
The company did the same thing with Operator, an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.
We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora, which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.
Apple’s Siri AI
When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.
However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like enginee

Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.”
That thesis resonates. Their events have been oversubscribed since day one. The second dinner party they hosted was covered by The New York Times. news.title: Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
news.summary_raw: Step one in convincing people to live with robots with cameras on their faces? Disguise them as cute home decor.
news.source_text:
You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.
It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.
As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.
That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.
“There are certain relationships in this era we want to fix between humans and our surroundings—human with nature, human with one another—every product is an experience trying to reconnect some of those relationships,” Wang says. Before cofounding OKA, he was a general manager at Meipai, a video-sharing app from the Chinese phone brand Meitu. He also cofounded Bondee, a now-defunct social media app that briefly went viral in Asia.
According to the company, the point of Mori, the nearly 12-inch-tall home robot lamp, is to reconnect its owners with nature. It can play nature soundscapes. It will glow different colors—inspired by rain, forests, fire, and wind—while reacting to your movements. It can guide you through a calming breathing session.

news.title: How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance
news.summary_raw: Learn how OpenAI built ChatGPT’s LLM-powered ad stack to understand conversational intent, keep ads separate from answers, and deliver relevant ads at scale.
news.source_text:
How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance
By Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam, Members of Technical Staff
Traditional advertising systems are built to respond to discrete units of user intent. A user searches for or views something online, the ads system receives those queries and page views as events, and the system looks for matching ads based on those events. Building an ads stack for ChatGPT was different: user intent develops across conversations and shifts over multiple turns of a conversation, sometimes without a fitting advertising moment. To support this new paradigm, we built a bespoke ads delivery system. This new type of ad stack is based on a custom, post-trained frontier LLM that makes tool calls for retrieval (identifying the top options), ranking (predicting user engagement), relevance (evaluating the usefulness of the ad), and running auctions for final ad selection and pricing.
Our ads system supports the nuance of evolving user goals by making three key design decisions: 1) implementing stateful ads sessions, meaning information is remembered across turns of a conversation and across multiple conversations, 2) relying on a custom, post-trained LLM that uses a tool call architecture to interpret a conversation’s context and underlying intent, and then effectively select, rank, and deliver ads, and 3) running the ads selection process separately from ChatGPT’s answer generation, in its own service, to keep ads from influencing answers and maintain ChatGPT’s neutral voice. We use our post-trained LLM to orchestrate the entire ads flow, determining the right ad to surface at the right time based on both the user’s current turn and conversation history. While bootstrapping a self-improving ads system like this used to take years, ChatGPT Ads reached $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launch; now, more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT since launch.
A conventional advertising request usually starts with a well-defined event. A user submits a search query or opens a webpage and the ads system receives a request. This type of system is fairly simple: it retrieves potential ad candidates, ranks them, runs an auction to appropriately price the opportunity, and shows the resulting ad to the user. ChatGPT does not naturally produce such a concrete moment.
In a ChatGPT conversation, people arrive with goals rather than a one-answer search query. They might be planning a trip, choosing software for their business, furnishing a home, or learning a new hobby. This doesn’t all happen in one turn of a conversation. ChatGPT often helps the user clarify what matters along the way.

news.title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
news.source_text:
AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.
Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.
A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.
Here's what changed, and what's next:
A drop-in compatible API
The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same:
use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app.
To get started, change your import statement:
- import FoundationModels
+ import AnyLanguageModel
The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.
Over the past year, we've added several major features:
- Tool calling works with every provider.
- Guided generation works with every provider, too,
including nested @Generabletypes and arrays of them.
- Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27.
On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with
any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol,
including Core AI models.
Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.
Hosted models, too
Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:
- OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs
- Open Responses, for any provider with a compatible endpoint
- Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options
- Google's Gemini API
- Ollama
- Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27
- Hugging Face Inference Providers, and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL
With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:
let model = OpenAILanguageModel(
    baseURL: URL(string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/")!,
    apiKey: ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["HF_TOKEN"]!,
    model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b",
    apiVariant: .chatCompletions
)
Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.
Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

news.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
news.summary_raw: Intermediate certs allow anyone to mint web credentials for any Internet server.
news.source_text:
Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet.
As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices.
One word: bonkers
The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here – Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide.
“This will be a massive cleanup job, bigger than Heartbleed,” Filippo Valsorda, a cryptography engineer and a cryptography maintainer for the open source Go programming language, told Ars. “There will be a very, very long tail, IoT devices, Docker containers, forgotten Linux machines, unmaintained CLI tools that shipped their own copy of the roots (which is common in some ecosystems, like Python). Also, Linux distributions are still rolling out updates, some of them are not ready yet, and then system administrators will need to apply them to a lot of machines.”
news.summary: Eight TLS certificates from eMudhra Limited have been compromised, allowing attackers to forge trusted browser and app credentials globally. This widespread flaw threatens all internet services, from web browsers to IoT devices, requiring immediate remediation.
news.enterprise_use: Go to your TLS/SSL management console and verify that none of the affected eMudhra intermediate certificates are in use on your infrastructure; if they are, replace them immediately with trusted authorities. Failure to act this week will expose your services to man‑in‑the‑middle attacks, credential spoofing, and potential regulatory breaches. This issue most directly impacts your Google Workspace, JumpCloud, and endpoint security configurations where certificates are used for authentication and secure communication.

news.title: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
news.summary_raw: Amazon Web Services logged attempts to leverage the internet-melting PHP2Shell bugs four days ago. They’re now being “broadly exploited” across the internet.
news.source_text:
The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.
Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.
But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.
AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.
“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.
Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, tells WIRED that the organization was unaware of AWS's research prior to publication and did not immediately have a comment on the findings. She added, “Although we agree that upgrading is absolutely imperative, to our knowledge, there has been no successful attempt at remote code execution.”
Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up, given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.

news.enterprise_use: S1: Inspect all servers and web applications on your cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) for PHP deployments and verify that the latest security patches are applied immediately. news.title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
news.summary_raw: The new open-source model speaks the language of DNA and can help researchers understand the effects of any changes on gene activity and health.
news.source_text:
The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop.
Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.
Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.
“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”
Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.)
DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works.
Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch.
Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA.
The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications.
Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the gen
news.summary: Hugging Face unveiled Carbon‑X, a new open‑source AI model that interprets DNA sequences through natural language chat, enabling researchers to query genetic information without extensive bioinformatics expertise. The model can run locally on standard hardware and is designed for small genomic queries up to 50,000 base pairs.
news.enterprise_use: Watch for potential integrations of Carbon‑X into genomic data pipelines or research workflows; it could reduce the need for specialized bioinformatics tools and accelerate hypothesis generation. Note that the model’s local deployment may reduce dependency on cloud‑based genomic services, impacting data‑transfer and storage costs in your environment.

news.title: Block’s new voice model sounds eerily human
news.summary_raw: Block said that the voice model can run locally on a MacBook M4 Max
news.source_text:
Jack Dorsey’s Block released a new voice model out of the company’s research lab that runs locally and sounds strangely human with its expressions like laughs, pauses, and cries. The company said the model, called Dessa, is trained fully on human speech and a single NVIDIA GPU rack.
Dessa is a full-duplex model, which means it can talk and listen at the same time, just like the GPT-Live model OpenAI released earlier this year. Typically, speech models are paired with a large language model for knowledge retrieval. Block said that Dessa’s knowledge stems from the conversational data it has.
Block said that the current models can sound unnatural and annoying because they have text in the pipeline that drives speech generation. A lot of models like ElevenLabs v4 or Fish Audio Drama 3 use voice tags to drive emotion in speech generation. Dorsey’s company claims that emotion is built into its model. It’s not clear if that emotion is being steered by some kind of tags.
“Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous,” the company said in a blog post.
The company’s researchers posted multiple examples of conversations with Dessa where the agent had different voices, cadences, and emotions. For instance, in the conversation, the bot said it was tired from work, and at that point it sounded tired.
In the example below, the bot was talking about the person making it comfortable while sounding emotional and almost breaking down.
Another one shows a Block team member playing a game with the voice assistant.
The company said that the model can run locally on a consumer-grade computer such as a MacBook M4 Max or better. However, there is no public access to Dessa at the moment, and Block has put out a call for safety researchers to test the model. This is likely to test out cases where a voice agent could trick people on the other end.
Block is in the business of finance and selling its solutions to small businesses. Square already uses voice AI to handle ordering. But with its own voice model that can run on-device, it can power a lot more business and consumer experiences at a lower cost.
news.summary: Block (formerly Square) has unveiled a new local voice model, Dessa, that can converse in real time with built‑in emotion and runs on consumer hardware. The model is still in research mode and has not been publicly released, with Block inviting safety researchers to evaluate its potential for deceptive interactions.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on Dessa’s development as it may influence future voice‑enabled IT support or customer service tools. Consider evaluating the model’s local‑runtime capability for on‑prem voice assistants in the next 30 days to assess any impact on your current voice or chat‑bot solutions.

news.title: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers
news.source_text:
Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers: The latest open image generation model from Black Forest Labs
Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.
Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:
You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
TL;DR
- One model for text-to-image, multi-reference image-to-image, and bounding-box layout control.
- The distilled checkpoint makes a 1024 × 1024 image in about 2 seconds on an H100.
- NVFP4 and FP8 weights load with from_single_file, for smaller GPUs.
- LoRA training scripts for both text-to-image and image editing.
- Ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline, so you can pop blocks out or add your own.
Contents
- Getting started
- What FLUX.3 can do
- Base model and quantized variants
- LoRA finetuning
- What it costs to run
- The architecture
- Modular Diffusers
- Try it
Getting started
Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):
pip install -U diffusers transformers
Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

from diffusers import ModularPipeline
pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein")
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.to("cuda")
pipe(prompt="a red fox", output="images")[0].save("fox.png")
What FLUX.3 can do
Text-to-image
FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. news.title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
news.source_text:
Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control.
“I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover.
More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960.

news.title: Digital Media Trends
news.source_text:
There are audiences, and there are fans. Fans represent a segment of consumers seeking long-term, consistent relationships with the intellectual property, artists, teams, and franchises they love.1 And while the media and entertainment industry is largely optimized around moments—blockbuster movie premieres, live sporting events, video game releases, and TV season launches—fandom isn’t experienced on the same schedule. Fans are willing to move across formats, platforms, and experiences during those big moments and in the “off-season,” in search of a continuity that they can’t experience otherwise. These fans may be signaling that the off-season isn’t a lull; it’s an opportunity.
This year’s Digital Media Trends research (based on a survey of 3,575 US consumers) focuses on self-identified fans—a subset of consumers who likely represent the industry’s most valuable and durable asset (see methodology). These fans and fan communities have already built connected, continuous ecosystems for themselves across multiple environments. But many say they’d prefer one environment that aggregates their favorite content, discussions, and experiences. If content providers and services want to capture more of those valuable interactions and remain central to the fan journey year-round, there may be an opportunity in orchestrating content and extending fandom experiences using nuanced knowledge about fans themselves. This integrated approach may be the key to retention and long-term return on investment for content providers.2 And generative AI may be the connective infrastructure that makes it possible.
The media and entertainment industry and its offerings continue to expand, giving consumers more options than ever across streaming video, gaming, social media, linear TV, music, podcasts, and more. But more choice has also led to increased fragmentation. Many consumers juggle multiple subscriptions and services, often paying for and using several just to access the content they want.3 As competition intensifies and consumer attention splinters, many media companies and content providers are looking for ways to grow their audiences, retain current users, and increase the time people spend within their environments.
In response, some media companies are broadening their offerings by introducing complementary podcasts and social videos, integrating chat and community features, or expanding their gaming or shopping capabilities4 to help drive more engagement within a single ecosystem. Deeper engagement, which can be measured by time spent, viewership numbers, breadth of content, interactions like shares, comments, and downloads, or in-app purchasing, can translate into higher advertising revenues, more consumer spending, and reduced churn.5
A majority of consumers (around 80%) are fans, categorized as those who self-identify as a fan of at least one entertainment category like TV shows, movies, gaming, sports, or music.6 Fans today follow creators, brands, and genres

The analysis suggests media firms could leverage AI to keep fans engaged year‑round and boost retention.
